summary: Describes a way to avoid blackholing traffic when the IGP is working on a link where LDP is not, by making routers keep the link from being preferred until LDP is ready. This matters for networks relying on LDP label switched paths, for example MPLS VPNs. This is an informational document, later updated by RFC 6138.

eli5.summary: If a road is open to cars but the bridge sign isn't ready yet, drivers get stuck. This memo says to avoid using that road until everything is ready.

questions: why does mpls traffic get blackholed
what is the maximum ospf link cost
subtitle: How a router can keep traffic off a link where routing is up but label switching is not, with no protocol changes.

tldr.problem: A link can be up in the IGP while LDP is not working on it. IP traffic would still use the link, but labeled (MPLS) traffic, such as VPN traffic, is blackholed.
tldr.mechanism: While LDP is not fully operational on a link, the IGP advertises that link with its maximum cost, so transit traffic avoids it but the link stays in the topology.
tldr.outcome: Labeled traffic is steered to other paths until LDP is ready. The mechanism is a local implementation matter and needs no protocol changes.

today: RFC 5443 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 6138 and RFC 10041, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: The Blackhole Problem
sections.content:
LDP builds MPLS label switched paths (LSPs) along the shortest path to a destination as determined by IP forwarding. In a common design, every link in an IGP domain (for example OSPF or IS-IS) has both an IGP adjacency and an LDP adjacency.

Services such as layer 2 or layer 3 VPNs depend on a complete edge-to-edge MPLS path between provider-edge routers. If even one link on the IP shortest path has no operational LDP session, a blackhole exists and services that depend on MPLS forwarding fail.

The RFC lists some causes: a configuration error, an implementation bug, or a link that has just come up and has an IGP adjacency while LDP has not yet established a session or distributed all label bindings. LDP itself cannot fix this, because it is not a routing protocol and cannot redirect traffic to another IGP path.
sections.eli5: If one road in a chain is closed to delivery trucks, the whole delivery fails, even though cars can still drive there. The trucks cannot choose a different road by themselves.

sections.title: Costing Out the Link Until LDP Is Ready
sections.content:
The root cause is that LDP follows IP forwarding decisions, but nothing couples the IGP state and the LDP state of a link. The fix is to discourage use of a link for IP forwarding as long as LDP is not fully operational on it. This is similar to RFC 3137, which lets an OSPF router advertise that it should not be used for transit, except that here it is applied per link.

In detail, the IGP advertises the link with its maximum cost. For OSPF that is LSInfinity (the 16-bit value 0xFFFF). For IS-IS it is 2^24-2 (0xFFFFFE), because a link configured with 2^24-1 is not advertised in the topology at all. The link is deliberately kept in the topology so IP traffic can still use it as a last resort in a massive failure.

LDP is fully operational on a link when an LDP hello adjacency exists, a matching LDP session is established with the peer, and all label bindings have been exchanged. A router generally cannot verify the last condition, so a simple strategy is a configurable hold-down timer; the RFC defines no default. When LDP End-of-LIB (then work in progress) is implemented, the timer is no longer needed, because receiving the End-of-LIB notification marks the session fully operational.

The mechanism needs no protocol changes and is a local implementation issue.
sections.eli5: The router puts a huge toll on the half-ready road so nobody picks it, but leaves it open in case every other road breaks. When the truck lane is finished, the toll goes away.

sections.title: When to Use It
sections.content:
The procedure fits networks where having working LDP-signaled LSPs, and avoiding blackholes for MPLS traffic, matters more than always choosing the best path for IP-forwarded traffic. MPLS VPNs and BGP-free core designs are the examples given. Non-optimal IP forwarding only happens briefly after a link comes up or when there is a genuine problem, and in the latter case an implementation should issue network management alerts so the operator can fix it.

It also needs alternate paths with enough bandwidth, since the costed-out link takes no transit traffic.

On a broadcast link with more than one IGP/LDP peer, the cost-out can only apply to the link as a whole, not to one peer. A policy decision is needed on whether losing LDP to one peer should divert traffic from all peers on the link.
sections.eli5: This is worth it when delivery trucks matter more than taking the shortest route for cars. It only works if there are other good roads to use instead.

sections.title: Interaction with TE Tunnels
sections.content:
Some networks use LDP together with RSVP-TE, which sets up traffic-engineered tunnels. Tunnel path computation uses a separate TE link cost flooded by the IGP. The RFC says the mechanism should be applied only to the regular IP link cost, to prevent unnecessary TE tunnel reroutes.

LDP LSPs across a TE tunnel need a targeted LDP session between the tunnel endpoints. That is the same problem as a regular link: if the tunnel is used for IP forwarding, its targeted session must be operational. Raising the IP cost of the tunnel while there is no operational session solves it. When there is no IGP adjacency over the tunnel and the tunnel is not advertised into the IGP, this is a local matter for the tunnel headend router.
sections.eli5: Special reserved lanes have their own price list. Only the normal price list is changed, so the reserved lanes are not moved around for no reason.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A denial-of-service attack that brings down LDP on a link, or stops it from becoming operational, could be one cause of blackholing. The RFC does not address how to prevent LDP session failure. Setting the IGP cost to the maximum on such a link is not expected to introduce new threats, since the operation is internal to the router.

Making many LDP links unavailable at once could still drop traffic because of limited remaining capacity. That could be triggered by operational or implementation error, and the RFC treats these as general security issues where implementors should follow current best security practice.
sections.eli5: Someone could break the truck lanes on purpose. The fix does not stop that, but it does not make it any worse either.
